analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans sold through insurance exchanges to spend at least 90% of premiums on medical care.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Keith Ellison's bill would bar any health insurance plan from being sold through a health insurance exchange unless at least 90 cents of every premium dollar went to actual medical care — what's called a medical loss ratio. The rest would have to go to customer service and administration, not overhead or profit. It applied to any exchange created or recognized under federal law, effective January 1, 2010.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying coverage through an exchange would get a guarantee that at least 90% of their premiums pay for care. If insurers couldn't meet the ratio, they would have to cut administrative costs, overhead, or profit margins — or rebate the difference to customers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any coverage from being offered through a health insurance exchange unless it is demonstrated to have a medical loss ratio of at least 90%, meaning at least 90% of premiums must go to medical expenses.
The requirement applied to exchanges at the national, regional, or state level, effective for coverage offered on or after January 1, 2010.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would bear the cost: plans with heavy administrative overhead or large profit margins would have to trim them or return money to customers. Insurers with lean operations would compete more easily.

drawbacks.text: A strict 90% ratio could squeeze out smaller insurers or plans that legitimately spend more on administration for special populations, and regulators would have to police how 'medical expenses' are defined and counted.
Because it only covered plans sold through exchanges, it would do nothing for the majority of people insured through employers or outside an exchange.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — forcing most of every premium dollar to pay for care instead of administration and profit — outweighs the administrative policing costs, but the bill was narrow: it covered only exchange plans, so most insured Americans would have seen no direct effect.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced H.R. 2833 on June 11, 2009, with three Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Jan Schakowsky, John Tierney, and Hank Johnson of Georgia.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on June 12 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action is recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off: no 90% minimum medical loss ratio was ever imposed on exchange plans, so no insurer had to shift overhead and profit into patient care or rebates. The final health reform law enacted in 2010 set lower loss ratio requirements (80-85%), leaving more room for administrative spending than this bill would have allowed.

for.name: Rep. Keith Ellison
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring a 90% minimum medical loss ratio for exchange coverage.

against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over health insurance legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral; it sat in the Subcommittee on Health for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with only Democratic cosponsors, and with Democrats controlling the House it went no further than a subcommittee referral; no votes were ever taken, so the record shows no formal opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have capped what insurers could keep for administration and profit at 10 cents per premium dollar on exchange plans, forcing cuts to overhead or rebates to customers. Insurers' business models rely heavily on administrative margins, so a 90% ratio is a direct cost to them and a direct savings for people buying coverage.
